items.title: Negatives, fractions and decimals in order
items.prose: Five amounts, some below zero and some written as fractions.
items.question: Put them in order, smallest first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each amount into a decimal, then place it on a number line.

byKey.o2: You put $-\tfrac13$ first. It is about $-0.33$, closer to zero than $-0.5$, so it is larger.
byKey.o4: You put $\tfrac13$ below 0.3. But $\tfrac13 = 0.333\ldots$, just above 0.3.
byKey.o5: You put 0.34 below $\tfrac13$. But $0.333\ldots$ has 3 hundredths and 0.34 has 4.

explain.text: As decimals: $-0.5$, $-0.333\ldots$, 0.3, $0.333\ldots$, 0.34. Among negatives, the one closer to zero is larger. Among positives, compare place by place.

items.title: Seven twelfths
items.prose: No power of ten works for twelfths, because $12 = 2 \times 2 \times 3$. Divide instead.
items.question: Write $\tfrac{7}{12}$ as a decimal, rounded to three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 7 by 12 one place at a time.

byKey.two-places: That is two decimal places. Give three.
byKey.flipped: You divided 12 by 7. The fraction means 7 divided by 12, which is less than 1.
byKey.digits: You wrote 7 and 12 side by side. Divide 7 by 12 instead.

explain.text: 70 tenths shared by 12 is 5 each, 10 left. 100 hundredths gives 8 each, 4 left. Then 40 gives 3 each, 4 left, for ever: $0.58333\ldots \approx 0.583$.

items.title: A week of P&L
items.prose: A strategy's daily P&L for one week is in the table. The running P&L was £0 before Monday.
items.question: What is the running P&L at the end of Friday, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the days one at a time, keeping each sign.

byKey.sign: You have the size right but lost the sign. The losses outweigh the gains.
byKey.sizes: You added the sizes and ignored the signs. Losses move the total down.
byKey.losses-only: That is the losses alone. Add the gains of £84.50 and £52.15 too.

explain.text: Running total: 84.50, then $-41.75$, $-79.55$, $-27.40$ and $-37.00$. Gains total £136.65 and losses £173.65, so the week ends £37.00 down.

items.title: The worst fall in that week
items.prose: Same week. The running P&L after each day was +84.50, −41.75, −79.55, −27.40 and −37.00.
items.question: What is the largest fall from a peak to a later low, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the peak minus the lowest point after it.

byKey.no-sign: You took 79.55 from 84.50. The low is −79.55, so subtract a negative: the sizes add.
byKey.one-day: That is the biggest one-day loss. The fall ran on into Wednesday, to −79.55.
byKey.last-day: You used Friday's close. The low came on Wednesday, at −79.55.

explain.text: The peak is +84.50 on Monday and the lowest point after it is $-79.55$ on Wednesday. The fall is $84.50 - (-79.55) = 84.50 + 79.55 = 164.05$ pounds.

items.title: A long and a short
items.prose: You are long 400 shares of A and short 250 shares of B. Today A falls by £0.35 and B falls by £1.12.
items.question: What is your total P&L for the day, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each position's P&L, then add them.

byKey.both-losses: You treated both falls as losses. The short in B gains when B falls.
byKey.both-gains: You treated both falls as gains. The long in A loses when A falls.
byKey.forgot-short: That is A alone. Add the short position in B, which gained.

items.title: Far along a recurring decimal
items.question: What is the 100th digit after the point?

feedback.correct: The 100th digit is the 4th digit of a block: 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count whole blocks of 6 first, then what is left.

byKey.block-end: You took the last digit of a block. 16 blocks fill 96 places, and 4 more reach 100.
byKey.off-by-one: You landed one place too far. After 96 places, the next four digits are 1, 4, 2, 8.
byKey.block-start: You assumed 100 ends a block. 16 blocks fill 96 places, so 100 is 4 places into the next.

explain.text: Each block has 6 digits. $16 \times 6 = 96$, so 16 whole blocks fill the first 96 places. Places 97 to 100 are 1, 4, 2, 8, so the 100th digit is 8.

items.title: Proving the sign rule
items.prose: Show that $(-5) \times (-4) = 20$. Use only: anything times 0 is 0, and a sum is multiplied part by part.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $(-5) \times 4 + (-5) \times (-4) = 0$, multiply the sum part by part

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the fact about zero.

byKey.k2: That line rewrites the 0 as a sum. Start from the plain fact about zero.
byKey.k3: You split the bracket before writing it. Write the bracket first.
byKey.k5: That is the conclusion, so it comes last.

explain.text: Start from $(-5) \times 0 = 0$ and write 0 as $4 + (-4)$. Splitting gives $-20 + (-5) \times (-4) = 0$. Only $+20$ cancels $-20$, so $(-5) \times (-4) = 20$.

items.title: Average price of uneven fills
items.prose: A buy order for 300 shares fills in two parts: 200 shares at £20.13 and 100 shares at £20.21.
items.question: What is the average price per share, to the penny?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the total cost, divide by 300 shares, then round.

byKey.simple: You averaged the two prices. More shares filled at £20.13, so it pulls the average down.
byKey.chopped: You cut after two places. The third digit is 6, so round up.
byKey.unrounded: Prices are quoted to the penny. Round to two decimal places.

explain.text: Cost: $200 \times 20.13 + 100 \times 20.21 = 4026 + 2021 = 6047$. Then $6047 \div 300 = 20.15666\ldots$, a recurring decimal. The third digit is 6, so it rounds up to £20.16.

items.title: Two mistakes with minus signs
items.prompt: A friend's trading account shows −£40. A £15 fee turns out to be a mistake and is removed. Your friend says: “Minus and minus make more minus, so I am now at −£55.” The same friend is short 100 shares, and the price falls by £0.60. They say: “The price fell, so I lose £60.” Explain both mistakes. Give the correct balance and the correct P&L. Justify each sign with the number line, a pattern or the part-by-part argument.
items.model:
**The balance.** Removing the fee takes away a charge of $-15$:

$$-40 - (-15) = -40 + 15 = -25.$$

The fee had moved the balance 15 to the left. Taking it away undoes that move. So the balance moves 15 to the **right**, from $-40$ to $-25$ pounds.

**The P&L.** P&L is position times price change. Short 100 shares is a position of $-100$. The price change is $-0.60$:

$$(-100) \times (-0.60) = 60.$$

The friend gains £60. They sold borrowed shares high and can buy them back £0.60 cheaper each.

**Why the product is positive.** Follow the pattern as the second number steps down by 1:

$$(-100) \times 1 = -100$$

$$(-100) \times 0 = 0$$

$$(-100) \times (-1) = 100$$

Each step down adds 100, so the pattern climbs past zero. Scaling by 0.6 gives $(-100) \times (-0.6) = 60$.

The part-by-part argument agrees. Since $0.6 + (-0.6) = 0$:

$$(-100) \times 0.6 + (-100) \times (-0.6) = 0$$

$$-60 + (-100) \times (-0.6) = 0$$

Only $+60$ cancels $-60$, so the product is $+60$.

**The mix-up.** The friend used one slogan for two jobs. For adding and subtracting, think of moves on the line. The rule that two negatives make a positive is for multiplying and dividing only.

rubric.text: Explains that removing a charge moves the balance right, because subtracting undoes adding.
Gives the correct P&L: $(-100) \times (-0.60) = +60$ pounds, a gain.
Justifies the positive product with a pattern, a story of undoing losses, or the part-by-part argument.
Names the mix-up: the two-negatives rule belongs to multiplying, not to adding or subtracting.
States units and signs clearly, in pounds, naming each result as a gain or a loss.
